Every first Sunday, Nkechi makes her mum's jollof rice in the tiny flat kitchen in Leeds, and every first Sunday she lets the bottom burn a little, on purpose.
"That crispy layer was the best bit," she tells Hana, scraping it into two bowls.
Six years ago she couldn't walk past the rice aisle. In her second year, when she still couldn't sleep or make it to lectures, her GP pointed her to a bereavement counsellor, and those Thursday sessions are part of why she can stand at this stove now.
Today she laughs telling Hana how her mum sang loudly and badly while stirring. Her eyes sting halfway through the story, and she lets them.
Later she video-calls her brother in Lagos to argue about how much pepper is too much, then goes back to her thesis draft. Her mum would have wanted it finished.

qa.q: What does Nkechi cook every first Sunday?
qa.a: Her mum's jollof rice, with the bottom left to burn a little on purpose.

qa.q: What shows that Nkechi now feels warmth as well as pain when she remembers her mum?
qa.a: She laughs telling Hana about her mum's loud, bad singing, yet her eyes sting halfway through and she lets them.

qa.q: What helped Nkechi when her grief stayed stuck, and why did it matter?
qa.a: When she still couldn't sleep or get to lectures, her GP pointed her to a bereavement counsellor, and those sessions helped her reach the point where the recipe brings warmth.

qa.q: What might the first-Sunday cooking mean for Hana?
qa.a: Hana gets to know Nkechi's mum through the crispy rice and the stories, and sees a friend carry on with life while keeping the memory close.

grounding: Shows years-later grief held with warmth through a kept recipe, alongside earlier counselling when the pain had stayed frozen.

passage:
At the community centre in Dehradun, the last child packed up her geometry box, and Sahil stayed back, wiping the whiteboard slowly.
Dolma, who runs the Saturday library next door, leaned in. "You always stay late. Why?"
"My father did," Sahil said. "He taught maths at a government school for thirty years and never left while a kid still had a doubt. He died when I was eighteen."
"Is it hard, doing his thing?"
"It was. For two years I couldn't even open his notebooks. The college counsellor helped me get unstuck." He smiled. "Now when a kid finally gets fractions, it's like he's in the room. It stings a bit and feels good at the same time."
Dolma nodded. "Six years is a long time to keep someone that close."
"He's in how I teach," Sahil said, capping the marker. "That's enough."

qa.q: What does Dolma run next door?
qa.a: The Saturday library.

qa.q: What does Sahil mean when he says it 'stings a bit and feels good at the same time'?
qa.a: He feels both the ache of missing his father and warmth that his father's way of teaching lives on through him.

qa.q: What helped Sahil when his grief was stuck, and what could someone in that place do?
qa.a: When he couldn't open his father's notebooks for two years, the college counsellor helped him get unstuck; anyone frozen like that could reach out to a counsellor too.

qa.q: How are the children at the centre affected by Sahil's habit?
qa.a: They get a teacher who stays until their doubts are cleared, so they benefit from his father's value without knowing its story.

grounding: Illustrates a continuing bond years after a death, kept alive through a parent's value, with counselling having helped earlier when grief was stuck.

passage:
Dear Vidya,
Today is four years since Ma died. I made her lemon rice this morning, the way she taught me, with too many curry leaves. It still doesn't taste exactly like hers.
You asked me last year whether it gets easier. It changes. For the first two years I couldn't even open her recipe notebook. I went to a counsellor for a while, because everything felt stuck. That helped more than I expected.
Now I laugh at her notes in the margins: "Pankaj, don't burn it." I still miss her. But I also live. I got the job, I moved cities, and I think she'd be proud.
Come over on Sunday? I'll make the lemon rice.
Pankaj

qa.q: What did Pankaj make this morning?
qa.a: Ma's lemon rice, with too many curry leaves.

qa.q: How does Pankaj seem to feel about Ma now?
qa.a: Pankaj feels warm affection alongside ongoing sadness, laughing at her notes while still missing her.

qa.q: What helped Pankaj move from feeling stuck to living fully?
qa.a: Seeing a counsellor when the grief felt stuck, and keeping Ma's recipe as a living habit.

qa.q: How might Vidya feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Vidya may feel comforted and hopeful, hearing that grief changes and that warmth can come back.

grounding: Shows a griever, years after a mother's death, keeping her recipe, remembering her warmly, and noting counselling helped when grief felt stuck.

passage:
Trisha, you asked why I always make chai with cardamom and a pinch of pepper. It's Dadi's way. She died five years ago, when I was twenty.
The first year was awful. I couldn't make chai at all without crying. I stopped going into the kitchen. My mother finally took me to a grief counsellor, and slowly, slowly, things moved.
Now? I make it her way every morning. Sometimes I talk to her while the water boils. "Too much pepper, Dadi?" It makes me smile more than cry now.
She also taught me to never let a guest leave hungry. So, Trisha, you're not leaving until you've had a second cup. That's Ayesha's rule, inherited from Dadi.

qa.q: What does Ayesha add to her chai?
qa.a: Cardamom and a pinch of pepper.

qa.q: How does Ayesha feel when she talks to Dadi while the water boils?
qa.a: Ayesha feels warm and fond, smiling more than crying, though the loss is still there.

qa.q: What helped Ayesha through the first year?
qa.a: Seeing a grief counsellor when the kitchen felt impossible, which helped the pain move.

qa.q: What might Trisha experience being told she can't leave without a second cup?
qa.a: Trisha may feel touched and welcomed, receiving Dadi's value through Ayesha.

grounding: Shows a griever, years after a grandmother's death, keeping her chai recipe and values with warmth as well as pain.

passage:
I've shared a flat with Uday for two years. His father died when he was nineteen, before I knew him.
Here's what I've seen. Every Sunday morning, Uday polishes his shoes on the balcony with an old brush. He told me once it was his father's habit, "Shoes tell people who you are." He hums while he does it.
On the anniversary in June, he took the day off and went quiet. I left him alone, then brought him dinner. He talked about his father for an hour, laughing and wiping his eyes.
I don't know what he feels inside. But he doesn't seem frozen. He seems like someone carrying his father with him. Eshaan, flatmate.

qa.q: What does Uday do every Sunday morning?
qa.a: He polishes his shoes on the balcony with an old brush.

qa.q: What does Uday humming while polishing suggest about his feelings?
qa.a: He seems to feel warm and connected to his father, keeping the habit with affection rather than only pain.

qa.q: What did Eshaan do on the anniversary that helped?
qa.a: Eshaan gave Uday space, then brought dinner, which let him talk about his father.

qa.q: How does Eshaan seem to see Uday's grief?
qa.a: Eshaan sees it as alive rather than frozen, noticing Uday carries his father with him while living his life.

grounding: Shows a flatmate observing a young man who, years after his father's death, keeps his habit and remembers him with warmth and pain.

passage:
First year, a Friday. Farhan stood in the kitchen with Abbu's steel ladle and could not lift it. Some days he did not open the shop at all. His sister Noor noticed, and that spring she went with him to a grief counsellor at the community clinic, week after week.
Third year, Eid morning. Farhan made Abbu's biryani, burning the bottom exactly the way Abbu used to. Noor tasted it and laughed, then both of them cried a little over the pot, and then they ate two plates each.
Fourth year, a Sunday. On the terrace Farhan handed his nephew a bowl of grain. "Scatter it wide, like this. These are Abbu's sparrows." The boy asked who Abbu was. Farhan smiled and told him, and the telling did not hurt the way it once had.

qa.q: What did Farhan hand his nephew on the terrace?
qa.a: A bowl of grain to scatter for the sparrows.

qa.q: How had Farhan's feelings about Abbu changed by the fourth year?
qa.a: He could feel warmth alongside the pain, smiling as he told the story, where once he could not even lift the ladle.

qa.q: What turning point helped Farhan move from frozen to carrying on?
qa.a: Seeing a grief counsellor with Noor when the pain had frozen him, and later keeping Abbu's recipe and sparrow habit alive.

qa.q: What might Eid morning have been like for Noor?
qa.a: Noor could laugh and cry over the burnt biryani with her brother, sharing the warmth and the loss together.

grounding: Shows a griever over years moving from frozen pain, with counselling, to keeping a parent's recipe and habit alive with warmth.
